passages.t: ‘May my prayer be set before You like incense’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). “I call upon You, O LORD; come quickly to me” (verse 1). Then a picture from the temple. “May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering” (verse 2).

The singer asks God to guard him from the inside out. “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips” (verse 3). “Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing” (verse 4). He does not want even to taste what wicked people enjoy: “let me not feast on their delicacies” (verse 4).

He will welcome correction. “Let the righteous man strike me; let his rebuke be an act of loving devotion. It is oil for my head; let me not refuse it” (verse 5).

Verses 6 and 7 are hard to follow (see below). Then the singer looks to God again. “But my eyes are fixed on You, O GOD the Lord. In You I seek refuge” (verse 8). He asks to be kept from traps, and that the wicked fall into their own nets “while I pass by in safety” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Incense was burned in the temple every morning and every evening (Exodus 30:7-8). Its sweet smoke rose up before God. The evening offering was made at the end of the day. The singer may be far from the temple, or simply at home at evening. Either way, he asks God to receive his prayer and his lifted hands as if they were those offerings.

Most psalms like this ask for protection from enemies outside. This one also asks for protection from the enemy inside: his own mouth, his own heart, his own appetite for what the wicked enjoy.

Verse 5 is striking. A rebuke from a good person is called ‘loving devotion’ and ‘oil for my head’, a sign of honour and kindness. It hurts, but it heals.

Verses 5 to 7 are among the hardest verses in the Psalms to translate. The Hebrew is short and some words are rare, and the text may have been damaged in copying. Bibles render them in quite different ways. It is honest to say that their exact meaning is uncertain.
passages.later:
John saw in heaven an angel offering incense “along with the prayers of all the saints” (Revelation 8:3). James wrote, “If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). Proverbs says, “The wounds of a friend are faithful” (Proverbs 27:6).

Jesus told his friends in Gethsemane, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41).
passages.asks:
Psalm 141 is a good evening prayer. At the end of the day, lift your prayer to God like incense, and ask him to guard your mouth and your heart.

Verse 5 asks something hard: can you take correction from a good friend as a kindness? Many of us would rather be flattered by the wicked than corrected by the righteous. The psalm asks for the opposite.
